title: SHE WAS PROMISED TO A MAN… BUT SHE WAS STILL SOMEONE ELSE’S PROPERTY. THEN THE BIBLE RECORDS A SEXUAL OFFENSE THAT MOST CHRISTIANS HAVE NEVER HEARD PREACHED.
paragraphs: SHE WAS PROMISED TO A MAN… BUT SHE WAS STILL SOMEONE ELSE’S PROPERTY. THEN THE BIBLE RECORDS A SEXUAL OFFENSE THAT MOST CHRISTIANS HAVE NEVER HEARD PREACHED.

Leviticus 19:20–22 exposes a disturbing intersection of slavery, sexual exploitation, unequal power, and ancient justice. But buried inside this difficult passage is a question that reaches all the way to the Cross: What happens when human beings treat someone as property, but God calls us to recognize their humanity?
There are Bible passages that comfort you.
There are passages that strengthen you.
And then there are passages that make you stop reading because something inside you whispers…
Wait. Did the Bible really say that?
This is one of those passages.
Somewhere in ancient Israel, there was a woman whose name Scripture never records.
We do not know her age.
We do not know her family.
We do not know whether she had ever experienced the freedom to make decisions about her own future.
But we know something deeply troubling about her circumstances.
She was a female slave.
She had been designated for a man.
And she had not yet been freed.
Then another man had sexual relations with her.

What follows is a law that raises uncomfortable questions about consent, responsibility, justice, human dignity, and the difference between what ancient Israel's legal system regulated and what God's ultimate purpose for humanity reveals.
And before you assume this is simply another strange Old Testament law that has nothing to do with your life, consider something.
There are people sitting in churches today who know exactly what it feels like to have their lives controlled by someone else.
People who were used.
People who were violated.
People whose suffering was minimized because someone more powerful controlled the story.
People who were told to remain silent because exposing what happened might embarrass a family, a ministry, or a respected person.
And some of them have spent years wondering whether God noticed.
So we need to read this passage carefully.
Not to sensationalize a woman's suffering.
Not to force modern assumptions onto an ancient text.
And certainly not to defend exploitation in the name of Scripture.
We need to listen to what the passage actually says, understand what it does and does not establish, and allow the whole counsel of Scripture to bring us toward Jesus Christ.
Because sometimes the passages we find most disturbing are the very passages that expose how desperately humanity needs redemption.
Leviticus 19:20–22 reads in the King James Version:

"And whosoever lieth carnally with a woman, that is a bondmaid, betrothed to an husband, and not at all redeemed, nor freedom given her; she shall be scourged; they shall not be put to death, because she was not free.
And he shall bring his trespass offering unto the LORD, unto the door of the tabernacle of the congregation, even a ram for a trespass offering.
And the priest shall make an atonement for him with the ram of the trespass offering before the LORD for his sin which he hath done: and the sin which he hath done shall be forgiven him."
Read those words again.
Slowly.
A woman is enslaved.
She is designated for a man.
Another man has sexual relations with her.
And the law discusses the legal consequences, including an offering made by the man.
If your heart feels unsettled, that discomfort deserves careful examination rather than an easy religious slogan.
But here is where responsible Bible study becomes essential.
The ancient Hebrew text contains details that are easy to misunderstand when we depend entirely on an English translation.
The woman is described as a שִׁפְחָה (shifchah), a female slave or bondwoman.

The passage also uses נֶחֱרֶפֶת לְאִישׁ (necherefet le'ish), a difficult expression traditionally understood as indicating that she had been assigned or designated to a man, often translated as betrothed.
That matters.
Because this was not an ordinary marriage arrangement involving two free individuals.
Her legal condition was fundamentally different.
The Hebrew also says:
וְהָפְדֵּה לֹא נִפְדָּתָה
Ve-hofdeh lo nifdatah.
Meaning, in context, that she had not been redeemed or bought out of her enslaved condition.
The verse continues:
אוֹ חֻפְשָׁה לֹא נִתַּן־לָהּ
O chufshah lo nittan-lah.
Or that freedom had not been granted to her.
There it is.
In the ancient language itself.
She had not been redeemed.
She had not been set free.
Her status mattered so much to the legal case that the text explicitly mentioned it.
And this brings us to one of the most difficult phrases in the entire passage.
The King James Version says, "she shall be scourged."
But the Hebrew expression is:
בִּקֹּרֶת תִּהְיֶה
Biqqoret tihyeh.
This expression is unusually difficult to interpret.

The noun biqqoret occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible, making its precise legal meaning uncertain. The King James Version understands it as a punishment, while many modern translations render it as an inquiry, investigation, or appropriate punishment.
That difference is significant.
We cannot responsibly claim that the Hebrew unambiguously commands the woman to be whipped.
Nor can we confidently reconstruct every legal procedure from these three verses.
And there is another detail we must face.
The passage does not explicitly say whether the woman consented.

It describes sexual intercourse within a deeply unequal social and legal relationship, but it does not supply enough information to determine the circumstances of consent or coercion in this particular case.
That is not a small distinction.
It would be irresponsible to declare, as a proven fact, that this passage describes a specific rape.
It would be equally irresponsible to assume that a woman living under slavery possessed the freedom, security, or bargaining power that a free person might have possessed.
The text leaves questions unanswered.
And sometimes faithfulness to Scripture means refusing to pretend that we know what God has not told us.
But what Scripture does tell us is troubling enough.
The woman's lack of freedom changes how the case is treated.
The law does not apply the death penalty in this situation, unlike the penalties prescribed for certain other sexual offenses involving betrothed free women in Deuteronomy 22.
The man must bring a ram as a guilt offering.
The priest makes atonement for his sin.
And the text says that he will be forgiven.
Now imagine hearing that as someone who has suffered sexual exploitation.
You might ask…
What about her?
Where is her voice?
Where is the account of her pain?
Where is the description of her future?
The passage does not tell us.
And we must not invent an answer merely to make the text feel easier.
But neither should we conclude that because this particular law does not describe her inner experience, her humanity was invisible to God.
A biblical law addressing a particular legal situation is not necessarily a complete statement of God's moral ideal.
That distinction matters enormously.
Ancient Israel's law operated within a society where slavery existed. Some laws restricted conduct, assigned responsibilities, and established penalties within those social conditions.
That does not mean every social arrangement being regulated represented the fullness of God's original design.
Jesus Himself teaches us to distinguish between certain concessions made within fallen human conditions and God's intention from the beginning.
In Matthew 19:8, while discussing divorce, He explains that Moses permitted certain things because of the hardness of human hearts, but that it was not so from the beginning.
We should not simply transfer that explanation mechanically onto every law about slavery.
But Christ's words establish an important principle: permission or regulation within a broken society must not automatically be confused with the highest expression of God's purpose.
So what was God's purpose from the beginning?
Before human beings built systems of ownership…
Before societies divided people according to status…
Before the powerful decided whose voice mattered…
Genesis 1:27 declared:
"So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them."
Male and female.
Both bearing the image of God.
Not one made in God's image and the other made to be disposable.
Not the wealthy bearing divine dignity while the enslaved possessed none.
Human worth begins with the Creator.
And that worth is not erased by poverty, captivity, abuse, social status, or another person's exercise of power.
Think about that woman again.
Her name was not preserved.
Her personal story was not recorded.
But the opening chapter of Scripture had already established a truth that no human institution could cancel.
She was a human being made in the image of God.
And that truth should make every believer tremble before treating another person as an object.
Because the moment we begin valuing human beings according to what they can provide us, we have already started moving away from the heart of biblical love.
Sometimes we do not need chains to enslave another person.
Sometimes we use fear.
Sometimes we use money.
Sometimes we use shame.
Sometimes we use religious authority.
Sometimes we manipulate someone's conscience until they believe that resisting mistreatment means resisting God.
And that last form of control is particularly dangerous.
Because when people use God's name to protect their own wrongdoing, they do not make their sin holy.
They add spiritual deception to it.
Maybe you know what that feels like.
Maybe someone once convinced you that your suffering was your responsibility.
Maybe you were pressured to forgive before anyone acknowledged the harm.
Maybe someone demanded your silence and called it submission.
Maybe you were told that protecting a powerful person's reputation was more important than telling the truth.
Hear this carefully.
Biblical forgiveness is not permission for continued abuse.
Repentance is not merely saying religious words while refusing accountability.
And grace does not require victims to pretend that evil never happened.
The same Bible that speaks about forgiveness also commands justice, condemns oppression, and warns those who exploit the vulnerable.
Isaiah 1:17 says:
"Learn to do well; seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow."
God does not instruct His people to admire justice from a distance.
He commands them to pursue it.
And when Jesus begins His public ministry in Luke 4, He reads from Isaiah and announces good news to the poor and liberty to the captives.
His mission is not reducible to a political program or a promise that every earthly injustice will disappear immediately.
It is the arrival of God's promised Messiah, bringing salvation and the liberating reign of God.
Yet His words leave no room for the idea that captivity, oppression, and human suffering are unimportant to Him.
Look at the people Jesus encountered.
He touched those society avoided.
He welcomed those religious gatekeepers despised.
He spoke to women whose voices were often disregarded.
He challenged hypocrisy.
He confronted those who burdened others while protecting their own appearance of righteousness.
And then there is the woman in John 8.
A woman brought before Jesus after being accused of adultery.
The religious leaders placed her in the middle of a public confrontation.
She was no longer being treated as a whole human being.
She had become a case.
An accusation.
An instrument in someone else's attempt to trap Jesus.
But Jesus refused to let their manipulation dictate His response.
He exposed the moral hypocrisy of the accusers.
And after they departed, He told her:
"Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more." — John 8:11, KJV
Notice both parts.
Mercy.
And a call to leave sin.
Jesus did not announce that sin was imaginary.
He did not say that holiness no longer mattered.
He extended mercy while calling for a transformed life.
That is the beauty of the Gospel.
Grace does not excuse evil.
Grace calls sinners out of evil.
And if we read Leviticus 19:20–22 through the larger biblical story, we must resist two opposite errors.
We must not pretend the passage is simple, harmless, or identical to modern principles of equal legal standing.
But we must not use its difficulty as an excuse to ignore the Bible's unfolding revelation of God's holiness, justice, mercy, and redemption in Christ.
The text tells us that the man brought an אָשָׁם (asham).
A guilt offering.
An offering associated with guilt and the need for atonement.
The Hebrew says:
וְנִסְלַח לוֹ
Ve-nislach lo.
"And he shall be forgiven."
Those words are important.
Because the law does not treat the man's behavior as morally insignificant.
It explicitly speaks of his sin.
He requires atonement.
He requires forgiveness.
But here we must be very careful.
The guilt offering was not a payment that purchased the woman's silence, nor does the passage say that the offering repaired every harm she may have suffered.
And forgiveness before God must never be twisted into a claim that an offender is automatically free from every human responsibility.
A person can speak about grace and still owe restitution.
A person can seek God's mercy and still need to confess the truth.
A person can claim repentance and still be accountable to lawful authorities.
The Gospel is not a hiding place for unrepentant abusers.
It is a summons to come into the light.
First John 1:9 says:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
Confession.
Not concealment.
Cleansing.
Not continued corruption.
Forgiveness.
Not a license to repeat the offense.
And now we arrive at the place where this ancient passage begins to point us toward something far greater than the legal system of ancient Israel.
Because Leviticus speaks of a guilt offering.
But the New Testament reveals the One whose sacrifice accomplishes what the old sacrificial system could never finally accomplish.
Jesus Christ.
Hebrews 10:4 declares:
"For it is not possible that the blood of bulls and of goats should take away sins."
The sacrificial system taught Israel about sin, holiness, guilt, cleansing, and the need for atonement.
But those sacrifices were not the final answer.
They pointed beyond themselves.
To the Lamb of God.
To the spotless Savior.
To the Son of God who entered our broken world, not as a sinner needing forgiveness, but as the righteous One who would bear the sins of His people.
Isaiah 53:10 even uses the Hebrew word asham in describing the suffering servant's life as an offering for guilt.
That connection is profound.
The guilt offering in Leviticus 19 does not mean that Jesus was the offender in that ancient case.
It means the biblical language of guilt and atonement ultimately finds its deepest fulfillment in the saving work of Christ.
He bore what we could not bear.
He accomplished what animal sacrifices could not accomplish permanently.
He opened the way for sinners to be reconciled to God.
But there is something even more astonishing.
The woman in Leviticus 19 had not been redeemed from slavery.
Her condition was described with language of not having been bought out of bondage.
Centuries later, the New Testament uses the language of redemption to describe what Christ has done for His people.
First Peter 1:18–19 declares:
"Forasmuch as ye know that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold…
But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot."
The Greek word translated "redeemed" in verse 18 is ἐλυτρώθητε (elytrōthēte), from a verb meaning to release or ransom.
It is not the same original-language word used in Leviticus.
And we should not pretend that Peter was secretly writing a direct commentary on this woman's particular case.
But the biblical theme of redemption creates a powerful theological contrast.
Leviticus describes a woman who had not been freed.
The Gospel announces that Jesus Christ has paid the price to redeem sinners from bondage to sin and bring them into a new relationship with God.
And this is where the story becomes personal.
Because perhaps you have never experienced literal slavery.
Perhaps you have never been trapped in the ancient legal conditions described in Leviticus.
But you know what bondage feels like.
You know what it means to be trapped in something you cannot seem to escape.
A secret addiction.
A destructive relationship.
A habit you promised God you would abandon.
A bitterness you keep feeding.
A shame that follows you into every quiet room.
A memory you wish you could erase.
An old sin that keeps whispering that you will never change.
Or perhaps you are carrying wounds caused by someone else's choices.
And you have spent years believing that what happened to you permanently reduced your worth.
Listen.
Your suffering is not the same thing as your sin.
What someone did to you is not automatically your guilt to confess.
You do not need to repent for being harmed.
And when Jesus calls sinners to repentance, He is not asking victims to accept blame for another person's wrongdoing.
He calls the guilty to turn away from sin.
He calls the wounded to come to Him for mercy, truth, and healing.
He calls all who trust Him into a life increasingly shaped by His righteousness.
That distinction may sound small.
But for someone who has spent years confusing shame with responsibility, it can change everything.
Because sometimes the deepest wound is not only what happened.
It is what you came to believe about yourself afterward.
That you are dirty.
That you are ruined.
That nobody will want you.
That God must be disappointed whenever He looks at you.
That your past has permanently disqualified you from a future.
But the Cross tells another story.
Not that sin is harmless.
Not that trauma disappears instantly.
Not that consequences are imaginary.
But that Jesus Christ is mighty to save.
Romans 5:8 says:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we made ourselves acceptable.
Not after we repaired every broken thing.
Not after we learned to sound holy in public.
Christ died for us while we were still helpless to save ourselves.
And that grace is not cheap.
It cost the blood of the Son of God.
Think about the Cross.
The One who never exploited anyone was stripped and humiliated.
The One who never abused power was condemned through an unjust process.
The One who never committed sin was treated as a criminal.
The One who possessed all authority chose obedience to the Father, even unto death.
He was not helpless before His enemies in the ultimate sense; He willingly laid down His life, as John 10:18 teaches.
And He did it to accomplish redemption.
Then the stone was rolled away.
The tomb was found empty.
And death itself could not hold Him.
This is not merely a story about a good man who suffered.
This is the Gospel of the crucified and risen Lord.
And His resurrection means that evil, guilt, and death do not get the final word over those who belong to Him.
Perhaps that is what someone reading this needs to hear tonight.
Your past may explain some of your wounds.
But it does not have authority to rewrite God's promises.
Your sins may have been real.
But Christ's mercy is real too.
Your suffering may have been severe.
But the Savior has not ceased to be compassionate.
And the story of your life does not have to end at the place where everything went wrong.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling injustice righteousness.
Not by demanding that wounded people smile through their pain.
But by bringing sinners to repentance, offering forgiveness through His sacrifice, restoring what sin has broken according to His wisdom, and giving eternal hope to everyone who trusts Him.
There is another side to this message.
And it may be the side that makes some readers uncomfortable.
Because not everyone reading this identifies with the powerless woman.
Some may recognize themselves in the person who used power selfishly.
Maybe you have controlled someone emotionally.
Maybe you have manipulated another person's vulnerability.
Maybe you have used Scripture to win arguments while refusing to obey it yourself.
Maybe you have wounded someone and then rushed to talk about forgiveness because you did not want to face accountability.
If that is you, do not hide behind religious language.
Come into the light.
Confess your sin.
Stop the harm.
Accept the consequences of your actions.
Make restitution where appropriate and possible.
Seek the help and accountability necessary to change.
And remember that genuine repentance produces fruit.
Grace is not opposed to accountability.
Grace is opposed to the lie that you can save yourself.
There is forgiveness in Christ for sinners who turn to Him in faith.
But there is no biblical promise that a person can deliberately cling to evil, refuse repentance, and use God's mercy as protection from judgment.
The same Savior who welcomed repentant sinners also warned people to turn from sin.
That is why this article is not merely about a difficult passage in Leviticus.
It is about what happens when we finally stop treating the Bible as a collection of comfortable quotations and allow it to confront the world we have built.
A world where the vulnerable are still exploited.
Where power still protects itself.
Where people still confuse legal permission with moral goodness.
Where religion is sometimes used to silence the wounded.
And where sinners still desperately need a Redeemer.
We cannot go back and discover the unnamed woman's complete story.
We cannot tell you what she thought, how she felt, or what happened after the legal proceedings described in Leviticus.
Scripture does not reveal those details.
But we can refuse to erase her humanity.
We can acknowledge the difficulty of her situation.
We can learn to read Scripture with humility rather than pretending every difficult question has a simple answer.
And we can look to Jesus Christ, in whom the righteousness, mercy, and saving purpose of God are revealed.
Galatians 3:28 declares that in Christ Jesus there is neither slave nor free, male nor female, with respect to their shared standing as those who belong to Him.
That does not mean every social distinction disappears overnight.
It means those distinctions do not establish different classes of worthiness before God in Christ.
And Philemon gives us a deeply personal glimpse of how the Gospel challenges relationships shaped by slavery.
Paul urges Philemon to receive Onesimus not merely as a slave but as a beloved brother.
The New Testament's treatment of slavery requires careful historical study, and these passages should not be oversimplified into claims they do not explicitly make.
But the direction of Christian discipleship is unmistakable.
The person standing before you is not merely useful.
Not merely expendable.
Not merely someone whose weakness you can exploit.
If that person is in Christ, you are looking at a brother or sister in the Lord.
And even if that person does not yet believe, you are still looking at a human being made in God's image.
Someone Jesus commands you to love as your neighbor.
Someone whose suffering should matter.
Someone whose dignity should not depend on their ability to defend themselves.
And now I want to ask you something.
Not as a theological exercise.
Not as a debate.
But as a question for your own heart.
Have you ever felt as though the world remembered what happened to you but forgot who you were?
Have you ever been defined by the worst thing someone did to you?
Have you ever looked at your own past and wondered whether God could still write something beautiful from it?
Or have you been the person who needed to stop making excuses and finally repent?
You do not have to tell the internet every detail of your wounds.
You do not owe strangers your private testimony.
But perhaps you can take one honest step today.
A prayer.
A confession to God.
A conversation with a trustworthy pastor or counselor.
A decision to seek safety.
A willingness to stop hiding behind appearances.
Or a simple cry from a weary heart:
"Lord Jesus, I need You."
You do not need to disclose anything unsafe or deeply personal to participate.
And if you see someone asking for prayer, do not treat their vulnerability as content.
Treat them as a person.
Pray for them.
Encourage them.
Point them toward Christ.
Because Christian community should be a place where truth is spoken with love, not where broken people become spectacles.
And if you know someone who has been told that their past makes them worthless, consider sharing this article directly with them.
Not to force them to talk.
Not to pressure them to forgive an unrepentant offender.
But to remind them that the Gospel is bigger than the lie that their suffering has erased their dignity.
You never know who might read it silently.
Someone who has not prayed in months.
Someone who has been avoiding church.
Someone who has never understood the difference between God's grace and human religious manipulation.
Someone who is quietly searching for a reason to believe that Jesus still welcomes sinners.
Invite your family, friends, fellow believers, struggling Christians, seekers, and even those who do not yet believe to follow along.
Not because following a page makes anyone a Christian.
But because hearing God's Word can lead people to encounter the truth about Jesus Christ.
And if this ministry has been helping you understand Scripture, grow in faith, or find encouragement during difficult seasons, I want to invite you to consider something deeper.
Not out of guilt.
Not because God sells blessings.
Those things cannot be bought.
Salvation is the gift of God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
But the New Testament also teaches that believers may voluntarily support those who labor in teaching and sharing the Gospel.
Galatians 6:6 speaks about sharing good things with those who teach the Word.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Some believers may prayerfully choose to include such support within their planned Christian giving, alongside their responsibilities to their local church, family, and other worthy needs.
Your giving should be voluntary, thoughtful, and rooted in love for Christ.
More Scripture-centered articles.
More discipleship materials.
More encouragement for believers who feel spiritually exhausted.
More opportunities to reach readers who may never walk through the doors of a church but will encounter a Gospel message on their phones.
Those free resources are part of why this mission matters.
Because not everyone can afford Christian books.
Not everyone has someone patiently helping them understand difficult passages of Scripture.
We want biblical nourishment to remain accessible.
Those products can be reminders of faith, useful discipleship tools, or meaningful gifts.
But they are not the heart of the invitation.
Jesus is.
The Word of God is.
The work of making disciples is.
You can pray.
You can read.
You can help bring Scripture into conversations that desperately need truth.
But before you leave this article, I want you to remember the woman in Leviticus 19.
The woman whose name we do not know.
The woman whose freedom had not been granted.
The woman whose circumstances became the subject of an ancient legal passage.
We should not pretend we know the rest of her story.
We do not.
But her presence in Scripture should remind us that difficult passages deserve serious study and that the people within those passages must never be reduced to theological props.
They were human beings.
Just as the people sitting beside us in church are human beings.
Just as the people wounded by our words are human beings.
Just as the people we disagree with are human beings.
Just as the people we are tempted to dismiss are human beings.
And every one of us must ultimately reckon with the God who created us.
The God who is holy.
The God who sees injustice.
The God who calls sinners to repentance.
The God who offers forgiveness through His Son.
The God who does not confuse religious appearance with genuine righteousness.
And the God who raised Jesus Christ from the dead.
So if you have been using your power to harm someone, repent.
If you have been hiding sin, come into the light.
If you have been carrying shame for something someone else did to you, do not mistake their guilt for your identity.
If you are weary, come to Christ.
If you are lost, turn to Him.
If you are already His, keep walking with Him.
Because the greatest miracle of grace is not that God calls evil good.
It is that God can forgive the guilty, restore the repentant, comfort the wounded, and make new people through the saving work of Jesus Christ.
And that is why we keep opening the Bible.
Even when its pages confront us.
Even when they disturb us.
Even when they force us to examine our assumptions.
Because we are not searching for a religion that simply tells us what we want to hear.
We are searching the Scriptures to know the living God.
And at the center of His redemptive story stands Jesus Christ.
Crucified for sinners.
Risen in victory.
Calling us to repent, believe, and follow Him.
The world may remember the scandal.
People may remember the failure.
Your own heart may remember the shame.
But when Jesus Christ redeems a life, the past no longer has the authority to write its final sentence.
The world may have written your name beside the wound, but Jesus can write your future beneath the word REDEEMED.
